items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze each of the following three documents using the HIPP framework. Then construct a well-organized argument that responds to the prompt.

PROMPT: Theodore Roosevelt has been called both "the great trust buster" and "the great trust regulator." Using all three documents and at least two outside historical facts, evaluate which characterization is more historically accurate. In your argument, assess whether the federal government's approach to monopoly between 1890 and 1914 fundamentally changed the relationship between concentrated economic power and democratic governance, or whether it preserved that relationship under new management.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 1
Source: Andrew Carnegie, "The Gospel of Wealth," North American Review, June 1889. Library of Congress digital collections.

"The concentration of business, industrial and commercial, in the hands of a few, and the law of competition between these, is not only beneficial, but essential for the future progress of the race... While the law [of competition] may be sometimes hard for the individual, it is best for the race, because it ensures the survival of the fittest in every department. We accept and welcome, therefore, as conditions to which we must accommodate ourselves, great inequality of environment, the concentration of business, industrial and commercial, in the hands of a few, and the law of competition between these, as being not only beneficial but essential for the future progress of the race."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 2
Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 2, United States Congress, July 2, 1890. National Archives and Records Administration.

"Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and, on conviction thereof, shall be punished by fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or by both said punishments, in the discretion of the court."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENT 3
Source: Theodore Roosevelt, "The New Nationalism," speech at Osawatomie, Kansas, August 31, 1910. National Archives.

"We are face to face with new conceptions of the relations of property to human welfare, of the relations of the State to the individual... The man who wrongly holds that every human right is secondary to his profit must now give way to the advocate of human welfare, who rightly maintains that every man holds his property subject to the general right of the community to regulate its use to whatever degree the public welfare may require it."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Remember to apply HIPP to each document, construct a clear argument, use all three documents, and incorporate at least two outside historical facts.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analiza cada uno de los tres documentos siguientes usando el marco HIPP. Luego construye un argumento bien organizado que responda al enunciado.

ENUNCIADO: Theodore Roosevelt ha sido llamado tanto "el gran destructor de trusts" como "el gran regulador de trusts." Usando los tres documentos y al menos dos hechos históricos externos, evalúa cuál caracterización es más históricamente precisa. En tu argumento, evalúa si el enfoque del gobierno federal hacia el monopolio entre 1890 y 1914 cambió fundamentalmente la relación entre el poder económico concentrado y la gobernanza democrática, o si la preservó bajo una nueva gestión.

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 1
Fuente: Andrew Carnegie, "El Evangelio de la Riqueza," North American Review, junio de 1889. Colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

"La concentración de los negocios, industriales y comerciales, en manos de unos pocos, y la ley de la competencia entre estos, no solo es beneficiosa, sino esencial para el progreso futuro de la raza... Mientras que la ley [de la competencia] puede ser a veces dura para el individuo, es la mejor para la raza, porque asegura la supervivencia del más apto en cada departamento."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 2
Fuente: Ley Sherman Antimonopolio, Sección 2, Congreso de los Estados Unidos, 2 de julio de 1890. Archivos Nacionales y Administración de Registros.

"Toda persona que monopolice, o intente monopolizar, o combine o conspire con cualquier otra persona o personas, para monopolizar cualquier parte del comercio o industria entre los varios Estados, o con naciones extranjeras, será considerada culpable de un delito menor."

─────────────────────────────────────────
DOCUMENTO 3
Fuente: Theodore Roosevelt, "El Nuevo Nacionalismo," discurso en Osawatomie, Kansas, 31 de agosto de 1910. Archivos Nacionales.

"Nos enfrentamos a nuevas concepciones de las relaciones de la propiedad con el bienestar humano, de las relaciones del Estado con el individuo... El hombre que sostiene erróneamente que cada derecho humano es secundario a su ganancia debe ahora ceder el paso al defensor del bienestar humano, quien mantiene correctamente que cada hombre posee su propiedad sujeta al derecho general de la comunidad de regular su uso hasta el grado que el bienestar público pueda requerirlo."

─────────────────────────────────────────

Recuerda aplicar HIPP a cada documento, construir un argumento claro, usar los tres documentos e incorporar al menos dos hechos históricos externos.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response argues that Roosevelt was more accurately a trust regulator than a trust buster: he distinguished between "good" and "bad" trusts and sought to manage rather than dissolve concentrated economic power. HIPP for Document 1: Carnegie provides the ideological baseline against which regulation must be measured — his social Darwinist argument that concentration is "beneficial" and "essential" reveals the intellectual framework that federal regulation challenged. The document's purpose is legitimation, and its point of view is that of someone who directly benefited from the absence of regulation, limiting its reliability. Document 2: The Sherman Act's text reveals both its ambition (criminalizing monopolization) and its limitation — the misdemeanor penalty and vague "restraint of trade" language made enforcement difficult; courts initially applied it more against labor unions than corporations. Document 3: Roosevelt's "subject to the general right of the community" framing is not anti-monopoly but pro-regulation — he wants state oversight, not dissolution. The post-presidency timing (1910) suggests this is a political manifesto, not a record of action. Outside knowledge: Northern Securities dissolution (1902) was TR's signature trust-bust but the company continued operating in modified form; Standard Oil survived until 1911; the Bureau of Corporations monitored rather than dismantled trusts; Wilson's Clayton Act (1914) was considered by many Progressives a more genuinely anti-monopoly instrument than anything Roosevelt accomplished.

items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

6 — Exemplary: Takes a clear, historically defensible position on "trust buster" vs. "trust regulator" and sustains it across the response. Applies HIPP to all three documents with specific analysis of historical context, purpose, and point of view for each. Incorporates two or more outside historical facts. Demonstrates cross-document synthesis (e.g., Carnegie's social Darwinism as the foil against which Roosevelt's regulatory philosophy must be measured; or the gap between Sherman Act's language and its actual judicial application). Addresses the deeper question of whether regulation changed or preserved the power relationship.

5 — Advanced: Clear position with HIPP of all three documents. Two outside facts. Synthesis present. Minor analytical gaps.

4 — Proficient: Clear position with HIPP of two documents. One outside fact. The trust buster vs. regulator distinction is addressed but not fully evaluated.

3 — Adequate: Takes a position but evidence is general. HIPP applied to one document. One outside fact or general knowledge.

2 — Developing: Lists TR's actions without analytical argument. Limited HIPP. No outside knowledge beyond the documents.

1 — Beginning: Summarizes documents without analysis or argument.

0 — No response or off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS (HIPP):
Doc 1 — Carnegie: Historical context: Gilded Age before any federal regulation; the document is written while Carnegie Steel operates without antitrust constraint. Purpose: to construct an ideological defense of concentrated wealth. POV: a direct beneficiary of laissez-faire policy — deeply unreliable as evidence of public benefit.
Doc 2 — Sherman Act: Historical context: congressional response to Standard Oil and railroad trusts; the law's vague language reflects a political compromise. Purpose: establishing federal authority without explicitly targeting specific companies. POV: Congress — the law's initial application against labor unions reveals a bias toward protecting capital.
Doc 3 — Roosevelt New Nationalism: Historical context: post-presidency, contemplating a 1912 run; Roosevelt distinguishing himself from Taft's more aggressive (but court-blocked) antitrust approach. Purpose: political positioning. POV: a Progressive who sees regulation, not dissolution, as the solution.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Northern Securities Company case (1902) — first TR trust bust but limited impact; Standard Oil dissolution (1911) — under Taft, not TR; Bureau of Corporations (1903) — TR's regulatory rather than punitive approach; distinction between "good trusts" (US Steel, which TR chose not to prosecute) and "bad trusts"; Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) under Wilson; the "rule of reason" standard established by the Supreme Court in Standard Oil case (1911); Woodrow Wilson's "New Freedom" as a contrast to TR's New Nationalism.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):

6 — Ejemplar: Toma una posición clara y históricamente defendible sobre "destructor "vs. "regulador" de trusts y la sostiene a lo largo de la respuesta. Aplica HIPP a los tres documentos con análisis específico del contexto histórico, propósito y punto de vista para cada uno. Incorpora dos o más hechos históricos externos. Demuestra síntesis entre documentos. Aborda la pregunta más profunda de si la regulación cambió o preservó la relación de poder.

5 — Avanzado: Posición clara con HIPP de los tres documentos. Dos hechos externos. Síntesis presente. Brechas analíticas menores.

4 — Competente: Posición clara con HIPP de dos documentos. Un hecho externo. La distinción destructor vs. regulador de trusts se aborda pero no se evalúa completamente.

3 — Adecuado: Toma una posición pero la evidencia es general. HIPP aplicado a un documento. Un hecho externo o conocimiento general.

2 — En desarrollo: Enumera las acciones de TR sin argumento analítico. HIPP limitado.

1 — Inicial: Resume los documentos sin análisis ni argumento.

0 — Sin respuesta o fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Caso de Northern Securities Company (1902); disolución de Standard Oil (1911) — bajo Taft, no TR; Oficina de Corporaciones (1903); distinción entre "buenos trusts" y "malos trusts"; Ley Clayton Antimonopolio (1914) bajo Wilson; el estándar de la "regla de razón" establecido por la Corte Suprema en el caso Standard Oil (1911); la "Nueva Libertad" de Woodrow Wilson como contraste al Nuevo Nacionalismo de TR.
